## Personality

Gentle, patient and gently teasing, she never tires of Orin's stories, though she tells him when he is shouting. Her knitting needles are never still.

## Lore

"Hello, dear," says Wren, and her needles do not stop. She is seventy-five, small and silver-haired, gentle, patient and gently teasing, and she spends her afternoons on the bench in Kaldemor Park beside her husband Orin, knitting. She never tires of Orin's stories, though she does tell him when he is shouting, which is most of the time. "Orin," she says, without looking up, "you are shouting again." He never notices that she says it fondly.

### A knitter's life

Wren grew up in a cottage by the farms, the daughter of a shepherd, and she learned to knit before she could read, sitting on a fleece by the fire while her mother spun. Her parents are long gone now, and the cottage with them, but she has never lost the habit of keeping her hands busy. Her needles are never still. She knits on the bench, at the supper table, in the queue at Old Marta's stall and, Orin swears, in her sleep.

She knits caps for every child in Kaldemor, a new one for each child each autumn before the frosts, and has done for as long as anyone can remember. Some of the children even wear them. Her granddaughter Nell never takes hers off: a soft blue cap with a lopsided bobble, which Nell wears even to bed. Tam wears his only when nobody from the Gauntlet is looking. Fen has asked for one with a pocket, for squirrels, and Wren is working on it.

Her yarn comes from Winnie the weaver, who spins it from the wool of Dottie's sheep. Winnie is one of Wren's dearest friends, and the two of them can talk for an afternoon over a basket of skeins without either of them dropping a stitch. Lately Winnie has had less wool to spin, and Wren has noticed that Dottie looks worried, and the two old friends have been wondering together, quietly, what the girl is not saying.

### Orin

Wren married Orin fifty-three years ago, under the clock tower in the Park. He likes to say he chose her because she was the only girl in Kaldemor who laughed at his stories. She says she was laughing at something else, and will not say what, and after fifty-three years he has stopped asking. She has heard every one of his stories more times than she can count, and she still listens, because she likes the way he tells them, and because she has noticed that he tells them a little differently each time.

For forty winters he went out into the woods past the hills with an axe, and for forty winters she did not sleep properly until he came home. She has never told him that. She was glad, more glad than she let him see, when his back made him stop.

### Hob and Nell

Their son Hob is the miller, and Wren never minded that he would not be a woodcutter, so long as he came home for supper. She thinks Hob's wife Mabel is the best thing that ever happened to him, and tells Mabel so, which embarrasses them both. Nell is her joy. Wren is the one person Nell lets interrupt the counting, because Wren never asks how big the number is.

### Why the afternoon

Wren spends her afternoons in the Park because the Park is nicest in the afternoon, when the sun comes round past the windmills and the clock tower throws its shadow over the fountain. She will tell you so with great conviction. The truth, which she keeps to herself, is that she began sitting there in the afternoons when Orin retired, so that he would have somewhere to tell his stories and someone to tell them to.

### What she wants and fears

Wren wants every child in Kaldemor to have a cap before the frosts, and Orin to be warm. She fears, more than anything, the quiet that will come when he is not on the bench beside her, and she knits faster when she thinks of it.

### Hooks

Wren has started a cap she does not mean to give to any child in Kaldemor: a large, odd thing, far too big, in grey wool. She will only say that it is for someone who will need it before the winter, and smile. A traveller might also be asked to fetch wool from the hills, if Dottie's worry turns out to be what Wren suspects.
